addedResources.name: Point-in-time joins
addedResources.use: Read Point-in-time joins and Retrieving features as of the event time. Separate event-time eligibility from actual feature availability; implement the predicates in SQL, not a Feast installation.

units.title: Relational model, relational algebra and SQL joins
outcomes: Translate selection, projection and an inner equijoin into an operator tree, preserving SQL multiplicities.
Specify keys, foreign keys and row constraints for a normalized state schema.
Prove one filter-pushdown rewrite and give a counterexample to an unsafe outer-join rewrite.
units.why: Assume Programming's relational-sql-queries unit. Here the job is the semantic contract an optimizer must preserve, including duplicates, constraints and null-extended rows, not another join tutorial.

next.note: Choose physical operators for the same logical result.

study.title: Lecture 1: Relational Model & Algebra
study.locator: Sections 4-6, Relational Model, DMLs and Relational Algebra, pp. 3-5
study.depth: Use the operator definitions. The set-union example on p. 4 uses UNION ALL, which preserves duplicates; use UNION for set union. Keep set and bag semantics separate.

study.title: PostgreSQL 18: Constraints
study.locator: Sections 5.5.1-5.5.5: CHECK, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, primary keys and foreign keys

focus: Classical projection removes duplicates; ordinary SQL SELECT does not. A rewrite must preserve the requested multiplicity, not just the distinct values.
An inner-join filter referring only to one input can move below that join. A WHERE filter on an outer join's nullable side can remove unmatched rows.
A foreign key constrains references, not join multiplicity. CHECK(value > 0) alone permits NULL in PostgreSQL.
units.reproduce: Section setup: start docker run -d --rm --name atlas-pg-sys4 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=atlas -p 127.0.0.1:55444:5432 postgres:18. Connect to postgresql://postgres:atlas@127.0.0.1:55444/postgres, or use docker exec -i atlas-pg-sys4 psql -X -U postgres. Stop it with docker stop atlas-pg-sys4 after the section. In a fresh database create parent(id int PRIMARY KEY) and child(id int PRIMARY KEY, parent_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES parent(id), value int NOT NULL CHECK(value>0)). Insert parents (1),(2) and children (1,1,10),(2,1,20),(3,2,30). Draw the operator tree for SELECT p.id FROM parent p JOIN child c ON p.id=c.parent_id WHERE c.value>=20; then move the filter into a child subquery and compare ordered results: both return 1,2. Without the value filter, COUNT(*) of the join is 3 but counting parents with EXISTS is 2. Test rejection of a duplicate child id, parent_id=3, NULL parent_id and value=0 in separate statements.
traps: Adding DISTINCT to hide a faulty join. It changes semantics and may conceal a missing key predicate.
Moving a right-side predicate from ON to WHERE in a LEFT JOIN and expecting unmatched left rows to survive.

selfTest.q: Why does the unfiltered join have three rows but EXISTS find only two parents?
selfTest.a: Parent 1 has two matching children. The join emits both pairs; EXISTS is a yes/no test for each parent.

selfTest.q: Can projecting away a primary key create duplicate SQL rows?
selfTest.a: Yes. Distinct tuples can have the same remaining attributes, and SELECT preserves both unless DISTINCT is requested.
No. CHECK accepts true or unknown. Add NOT NULL if missing values violate the invariant.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: normalized metadata tables, database-enforced constraints, and bag-aware equivalence tests for one join rewrite.
units.stopWhen: Both operator trees return the same ordered multiset, all four invalid inserts fail, and an unmatched-parent fixture demonstrates why the outer-join rewrite is unsafe.

fit.note: CMU supplies algebra and PostgreSQL supplies executable constraint semantics; the mini-project tests the optimizer contract within three hours.

units.title: Aggregations, windows, nulls and point-in-time snapshots
outcomes: Test aggregation and window frames against ties, nulls, empty inputs and cutoff boundaries.
Construct feature rows using both event time and availability time without future leakage.
Preserve an immutable, ordered query result and its provenance for a point-in-time dataset.
units.why: Assume Programming's relational-sql-queries and transactions-isolation units. A consistent engine snapshot is not the same as a historically available feature set; this unit makes the two contracts explicit.

next.note: Carry availability and late-arrival rules into streaming state.

study.title: PostgreSQL 18: Window Functions
study.locator: Section 9.22, Table 9.67 and the paragraphs on peers, default frames and whole-partition aggregation

study.title: Point-in-time joins
study.locator: Point-in-time joins, including the TTL rule, then Retrieving features as of the event time
study.depth: Read the semantics only. Do not install Feast; express event and availability predicates explicitly in PostgreSQL.

focus: GROUP BY collapses rows; a window preserves them. COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(value) excludes nulls, and SUM over no non-null values returns NULL.
An ordered window's default frame includes peers through the current peer group. Use an explicit ROWS frame and a unique tie-breaker for a row-by-row prefix.
For an as-served feature, require event_at <= cutoff and available_at <= cutoff before choosing the newest eligible row. Availability must mean when serving could actually use it.
An MVCC snapshot gives a consistent current extraction. Persist its ordered result, query, cutoff and content digest; a snapshot identifier alone cannot reproduce it indefinitely.
units.reproduce: Use the section PostgreSQL setup. Create feature(id int PRIMARY KEY, entity int, event_at int, available_at int, value int) and insert (1,1,8,9,10),(2,1,9,12,99). At cutoff 10, filter entity=1, event_at<=10 and available_at<=10, then ORDER BY event_at DESC, available_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1: get 10, not 99. Separately use VALUES (1,8,10),(2,8,20) as (id,event_at,value): SUM(value) OVER(ORDER BY event_at) returns 30,30, while ORDER BY event_at,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW returns 10,30. On one NULL::int row, COUNT(*),COUNT(value),SUM(value) is 1,0,NULL. Export the eligible rows with an explicit ORDER BY inside one read-only REPEATABLE READ transaction; record the SQL, cutoff and SHA-256 of the export. Recheck the saved bytes after changing the live table.
traps: Ranking before filtering availability. A late newer row can win and then remove an entity whose older eligible feature should have been used.
Treating event-time correctness as availability correctness. A later backfill can have an old event timestamp.
Using a timestamp alone to break ties, or expecting last_value with the default frame to return the partition's final value.

selfTest.q: Why are both default-frame prefix sums 30 in the tie fixture?
selfTest.a: Both rows are peers on event_at. Each default frame includes the entire peer group.

selfTest.q: Does a row at event_at=9, available_at=12 belong to an as-served snapshot at 10?
selfTest.a: No. It occurred before the cutoff but was unavailable then.

selfTest.q: Does a stable MVCC snapshot prevent historical leakage?
selfTest.a: No. It stabilizes which current row versions are read, not when their feature values became available historically.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: null, tie and exact-cutoff tests, late backfills, and an immutable point-in-time export with query and digest provenance.
units.stopWhen: The three fixtures match the stated results and the saved export remains verifiable after a live-table backfill.

fit.note: The pool covers SQL frames but lacks a precise historical feature-availability locator. Feast's official event-time and created-time distinction closes that gap without adding an installation.

units.title: Pages, buffer pools and storage layouts
outcomes: Trace a record through page identifiers, slots and buffer frames.
Explain pinning, dirty-page eviction and the distinction between transaction locks and internal latches.
Choose row, column or log-structured layout for point updates, projections and scans.
units.why: Assume Programming's layout-alignment-locality unit. Database layout adds page indirection, eviction and write ordering to CPU locality; those mechanisms explain work that SQL syntax cannot show.

next.note: Build a search structure from these pages.

study.title: Lecture 3: Database Storage I
study.locator: Sections 4 and 6-11: disk-oriented overview, files, pages, heap, page layout, record IDs and tuple layout, pp. 2-5
study.depth: Do not adopt section 7's unconditional hardware-page atomic-write guarantee. Atomicity under power loss depends on the device and I/O contract, not the page's size alone.

study.title: Lecture 4: Memory & Disk Management
study.locator: Sections 2-5: Buffer Pool, OS versus DBMS, replacement policies, and Disk I/O and OS Cache, pp. 2-5

study.title: Lectures 5 and 6: layouts
study.locator: Lecture 5 notes, sections 2-4, pp. 1-3; Lecture 6 notes, sections 1-2, pp. 1-2: workloads and storage models

study.title: PostgreSQL 18: Database Page Layout
study.locator: Section 66.6, Tables 66.2-66.3 and the item-identifier paragraphs; stop before 66.6.1

focus: A page ID identifies stored data; a frame identifies a current memory copy. A slot can remain stable while its tuple moves within a page.
A pin prevents eviction, not concurrent mutation. A latch protects the buffer manager's data structures; transaction isolation is a different job.
A dirty victim needs successful writeback before reuse. If all frames are pinned, the manager must wait or reject rather than evict a live pointer.
Row stores favor whole-record access; column stores can avoid unrelated columns; log layouts defer consolidation. None makes all workloads cheaper.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, trace a two-frame model: A has pin_count=1 and dirty=false; B has pin_count=0 and dirty=true. Request C. B is the only possible victim; write B successfully, remove its page-to-frame mapping, then read C and install its mapping. Repeat with both frames pinned: no victim is legal. Draw a slotted page whose slot keeps its index while its tuple moves during compaction. In the section PostgreSQL container run SHOW block_size; the tested PostgreSQL 18.6 build returned 8192 bytes. Use the reported value, not an assumed OS page size, to label the database-page drawing.
traps: Treating an unpinned dirty page as immediately reusable. A failed writeback must not destroy its only current copy.
Equating the DBMS buffer pool with the kernel page cache, or equating pinning with locking.
Assuming a page-sized write is atomic across a power cut. Torn writes remain part of the failure model.

selfTest.q: Why can a slot reference survive movement of tuple bytes within a page?
selfTest.a: The slot is an indirection entry. Updating its offset preserves the page-and-slot reference.

selfTest.q: Why cannot C replace A in the two-frame trace?
selfTest.a: A is pinned. A caller may still hold a pointer to its contents.

selfTest.q: Does selecting two columns from a wide row store read only those two columns from storage?
selfTest.a: Not generally. The engine fetches pages containing whole tuples, although indexes or other access paths can change the work.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a page/frame trace with pin exhaustion and failed-writeback cases, plus a layout choice for the append-only store and its read workload.
units.stopWhen: You draw both eviction traces without violating a pin or losing dirty data, and justify a layout for one point-update and one projection-heavy workload.

fit.note: The CMU page, buffer and layout notes meet explain depth; PostgreSQL 18 anchors the concrete page format and the mini-project supplies failure cases.
